questions.stem: ORGANIC CHEMISTRY is the chemistry of which element's compounds (with hydrogen + some others)?
questions.explanation: ORGANIC CHEMISTRY = chemistry of CARBON compounds (except CO, CO₂, carbonates, cyanides, carbides — these are considered inorganic). Carbon is special because of CATENATION (ability to form long chains + rings — C-C bonds are very stable, ~347 kJ/mol), TETRAVALENCY (can form 4 bonds), and its ability to form SINGLE, DOUBLE, and TRIPLE bonds. Over 10 million known organic compounds vs ~300k inorganic. FRIEDRICH WÖHLER (1828) accidentally synthesised UREA (NH₂CONH₂) from ammonium cyanate — first organic compound made from inorganic starting materials → destroyed the 'VITAL FORCE THEORY' (that organic compounds required a living 'vital force'). Today all life is known to be carbon-based. Organic chem branches: hydrocarbons (alkanes/alkenes/alkynes), alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, acids, esters, amines, amides, ethers, aromatics.

questions.stem: The simplest HYDROCARBON and the main component of NATURAL GAS + biogas is:
questions.explanation: METHANE (CH₄) — simplest alkane (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ series). Colourless, odourless (mercaptans added for leak detection). Main component (70-90%) of NATURAL GAS + BIOGAS (also CO₂, small amounts of other gases). Also present in MARSH GAS (decomposition of vegetation in water), FIREDAMP (coal mines — explosive), RICE PADDIES (bacterial methanogenesis), CATTLE BELCH (~4% of global methane). Greenhouse gas — 80× more warming than CO₂ over 20 years (but shorter atmospheric lifetime ~12 years). Burns in O₂: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat. Alkane nomenclature (first 10): Meth-, Eth-, Prop-, But-, Pent-, Hex-, Hept-, Oct-, Non-, Dec-. CNG (Compressed Natural Gas): vehicle fuel, mostly methane. LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas): mostly propane + butane. Shale gas revolution in USA made natural gas cheap since 2010s.

questions.stem: The IUPAC name of ACETIC ACID (vinegar's main component) is:
questions.explanation: ACETIC ACID = ETHANOIC ACID (IUPAC) = CH₃COOH. First 4 carboxylic acids (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH — but name based on total carbons): METHANOIC ACID (HCOOH — formic acid, found in ant/bee stings, nettle leaves — from Latin 'formica' = ant); ETHANOIC ACID (CH₃COOH — vinegar ~5-8% when dilute); PROPANOIC ACID (CH₃CH₂COOH — preservative E280); BUTANOIC ACID (rancid butter smell). Also common acids in biology: LACTIC ACID (milk, muscle), CITRIC ACID (citrus, TCA cycle), OXALIC ACID (spinach), MALIC ACID (apples), TARTARIC ACID (grapes, tamarind), ASCORBIC (Vit C), URIC ACID (gout when deposited as crystals in joints). Vinegar made from fermentation — ethanol → ethanoic acid via Acetobacter bacteria.

questions.stem: ETHYL ALCOHOL (the drinkable alcohol) and METHYL ALCOHOL (the toxic wood alcohol) differ by:
questions.explanation: METHANOL (CH₃OH, 'methyl alcohol', 'wood alcohol' — originally distilled from wood): TOXIC (even small amounts cause blindness, death — metabolised to formaldehyde + formic acid in body). Industrial uses: solvent, fuel, formaldehyde production. ETHANOL (C₂H₅OH, 'ethyl alcohol', 'drinking alcohol'): the only alcohol safe for human consumption (still intoxicating + carcinogenic long-term, but not acutely fatal in small doses). Made by fermentation of sugars (yeasts) or industrially from ethylene. Uses: alcoholic beverages, solvent, fuel (E85 ethanol-gasoline), hand sanitisers (60-70%), antiseptic. Spurious liquor tragedies in India = methanol contamination (common illegal distilleries). HIGHER alcohols: Propanol (3C), Butanol (4C), etc. Isomers: n- (straight chain), iso- (branched). ethyl = 2C, methyl = 1C.

questions.stem: BENZENE (C₆H₆) is the simplest AROMATIC hydrocarbon. Its structure features:

options.option_text: A hexagonal ring of 6 carbons with alternating single/double bonds

questions.explanation: BENZENE — discovered 1825 by MICHAEL FARADAY. Structure elucidated 1865 by FRIEDRICH AUGUST KEKULÉ (claimed inspiration from a dream of a snake biting its tail — ouroboros). Hexagonal planar ring, 6 carbons with alternating C=C and C-C bonds — but in reality ALL bonds are EQUIVALENT due to DELOCALISED π electrons (resonance hybrid). Represented as hexagon with circle inside. 3 pairs of delocalised electrons (6 π electrons). AROMATICITY criteria (Hückel's rule): planar, cyclic, continuous conjugation, 4n+2 π electrons (n=0,1,2... — so 2, 6, 10, 14...). Benzene = n=1 (6 π electrons). Benzene + derivatives (toluene = methylbenzene, xylene, phenol, aniline, naphthalene) are called AROMATICS — many have distinctive aromas (from which the class gets its name). Today: 'aromatic' is a formal structural term; not all aromatics smell pleasant.

questions.stem: FORMALIN (used to preserve biological specimens) is an aqueous solution of:
questions.explanation: FORMALIN = 37-40% aqueous FORMALDEHYDE (HCHO, methanal) + typically 10-12% methanol to stabilise. Uses: preservation of biological specimens (fixes tissues by cross-linking proteins), embalming, disinfectant, germicide. Carcinogenic — restricted use. FORMALDEHYDE is the simplest ALDEHYDE. Aldehyde general formula: R-CHO. Common aldehydes: HCHO (formaldehyde/methanal), CH₃CHO (acetaldehyde/ethanal — oxidation of ethanol causes 'hangover'), CHO-CHO (glyoxal), Benzaldehyde (almond smell). KETONES have R-CO-R': ACETONE (propanone, CH₃COCH₃ — nail polish remover), METHYL ETHYL KETONE. Distinguishing ald vs ketone: Tollens' reagent (silver mirror test — aldehyde +, ketone −), Fehling's/Benedict's (aldehyde + for aliphatic, ketone −). Uses of formaldehyde: Bakelite, plywood, textiles. typically 37-40%; methanal, HCHO.

questions.stem: POLYTHENE (PE) — the most widely used plastic — is a polymer of:
questions.explanation: POLYTHENE / POLYETHYLENE (PE) = polymer of ETHYLENE (ethene, H₂C=CH₂): n(C₂H₄) → -(CH₂-CH₂)ₙ-. Most produced plastic globally (~100 million tonnes/year). Grades: LDPE (Low-Density — plastic bags, squeeze bottles, film), HDPE (High-Density — milk jugs, pipes, detergent bottles — stronger, opaque). Other major polymers: POLYPROPYLENE (PP — from propylene; yogurt cups, bottle caps); POLYSTYRENE (PS — thermocol, disposable cups, CD cases); PVC (polyvinyl chloride — pipes, flooring; from vinyl chloride which is a carcinogen); POLYESTER/PET (bottles, fabric — from terephthalic acid + ethylene glycol); TEFLON (PTFE — non-stick; from tetrafluoroethylene); NYLON (from diamines + dicarboxylic acids); BAKELITE (phenol + formaldehyde — FIRST synthetic plastic, 1907 by Leo Baekeland — thermosetting). Polymers: repeating MONOMER units via addition or condensation. ethene, C₂H₄.

questions.stem: The 4 major classes of BIOMOLECULES in living organisms are:
questions.explanation: FOUR major biomolecules: (1) CARBOHYDRATES (sugars, starches — (CH₂O)ₙ; energy + structural). Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose) → Disaccharides (sucrose = glu+fru, lactose = glu+gal, maltose = glu+glu) → Polysaccharides (starch — plant storage, glycogen — animal storage, cellulose — plant cell wall, chitin — fungi/arthropods). (2) PROTEINS (chains of ~20 amino acids, folded 3D). Enzymes, hormones, structural (collagen, keratin), transport (hemoglobin), defence (antibodies). (3) LIPIDS (insoluble in water). Triglycerides, phospholipids, steroids, waxes. Energy storage, membranes, hormones. (4) NUCLEIC ACIDS (DNA, RNA — chains of nucleotides). Store + transmit genetic information. Also: VITAMINS + MINERALS are NOT biomolecules per the traditional classification — they're micronutrients (although vitamins are organic compounds). WATER is inorganic but essential (60% of body).

questions.stem: Functional group identification: -COOH (carboxylic acid), -OH (hydroxyl), -CHO (aldehyde), -NH₂ (amine). Which functional group is found in ACETONE?
questions.explanation: ACETONE = PROPAN-2-ONE = (CH₃)₂CO. A KETONE — characterised by the CARBONYL group (C=O) in the MIDDLE of a carbon chain. General ketone: R-CO-R'. Aldehydes have C=O at the END (R-CHO, always with at least one H on the carbonyl carbon). KEY FUNCTIONAL GROUPS (memorise): -OH = alcohol/hydroxyl; -CHO = aldehyde; -CO- = ketone; -COOH = carboxylic acid; -COO- = ester/carboxylate; -NH₂ = amine (primary); -O- = ether; -CONH₂ = amide; C=C = alkene; C≡C = alkyne; -NO₂ = nitro; -X (F/Cl/Br/I) = halide; -SO₃H = sulphonic acid; C6H5- = phenyl (benzene ring). Suffixes: -ol (alcohol), -al (aldehyde), -one (ketone), -oic acid (carboxylic), -yl (radical).

questions.stem: Which of the following is used as a 'LAUGHING GAS' in anaesthesia (also a greenhouse gas)?
questions.explanation: NITROUS OXIDE (N₂O) — 'LAUGHING GAS'. Discovered 1772 by Joseph Priestley. Anaesthetic properties noted by Humphry Davy (1800), who coined the name due to giggling effects. First clinical use as dental anaesthetic: Horace Wells (1844, USA). Still used today in dental + obstetric anaesthesia (in 50:50 N₂O/O₂ mixture, 'Entonox'). Also used as an oxidiser in rockets + whipped-cream aerosol propellant. GREENHOUSE GAS: ~300× more warming than CO₂ per kg, ~114-year atmospheric lifetime. Main sources: agricultural N fertilisers, livestock, industrial emissions. DISCOVERED: Methane (Volta 1776), CO₂ (Joseph Black 1754), Hydrogen (Henry Cavendish 1766), Oxygen (Joseph Priestley 1774, also Carl Scheele 1772 independently). OTHER INHALATION ANAESTHETICS: Ether (1842 by Crawford Long), Chloroform (1847 James Young Simpson for childbirth), Halothane (1956), Isoflurane, Sevoflurane (modern).
